cues.text: Suspected of a Foreign Loyalty
When war broke out between the Roman and Persian empires around 337, the Christians of Sasanian Persia found themselves suddenly and dangerously suspect.

Their faith, shared with the newly Christian Roman emperor Constantine and his successors, made them appear to many at the Persian court as a fifth column loyal to the enemy rather than genuine subjects of King Shapur II .
This suspicion was sharpened further by the simple accident of shared religion.

Constantine's own Roman Empire had only recently embraced Christianity as its favored faith, making every Persian Christian appear, in the eyes of a wartime court, a potential sympathizer with the enemy across the border.
The Christian community's own recent growth under earlier, more tolerant Persian kings had done nothing to prepare it for so sudden and complete a reversal of royal favor.
A Bishop's Refusal
Seeking funds for his war effort, Shapur demanded that the Christian community pay a crushing double tax.
He ordered Simeon bar Sabbae , bishop of the Persian Church's capital at Seleucia-Ctesiphon, to collect it from his own impoverished flock.
Simeon's refusal, understood by the king as an act of open defiance, transformed simmering suspicion into outright persecution.
A Bishop and His Clergy Martyred
Simeon was arrested, brought before the king, and, according to the earliest surviving accounts, refused every pressure to worship the sun in place of Christ.
He was beheaded on Good Friday together with a hundred of his own clergy, including two elderly priests who insisted on dying alongside their bishop.
They chose this rather than the more merciful death by strangulation the king had privately offered them.
Before his own execution, Simeon is remembered as having comforted his clergy with the assurance that death itself held no true terror for those who died confessing Christ.
This conviction steadied the resolve of the hundred priests and deacons who followed him to the same scaffold.
A Persecution That Widened
Simeon's martyrdom marked only the beginning of a persecution that widened in the years that followed across the Persian realm.
It claimed clergy and laity alike, among them, by later tradition, Simeon's own sister Tarbo .
She was martyred with a group of consecrated women on the false accusation of having caused the king's illness through sorcery.
Four Decades of Intermittent Violence
The persecution continued across nearly the whole of Shapur's long reign, with periods of relative calm interspersed with renewed waves of violence.
It was driven less by any single sustained royal policy than by recurring suspicion of Christian disloyalty during Persia's repeated wars with Rome.
A Zoroastrian priesthood that had long resented the Church's growing influence at court and among the nobility encouraged it throughout.
Legacy
Modern estimates suggest that tens of thousands of Persian Christians died during the roughly forty years of intermittent persecution associated with Shapur's reign.
This toll placed the ancient Church of the East, however briefly, among the most heavily persecuted Christian communities the ancient world had yet produced.
The martyrdom of Simeon bar Sabbae and his companions remains, to this day, one of the foundational memories of the Church of the East.
Within a few short centuries, that community would carry the Gospel along the Silk Road as far as Central Asia and China.
In hindsight, this missionary reach makes their endurance look like the seed of something far larger than the persecution ever imagined it could contain.
Every later Christian community that has had to rebuild its life from scratch after violent suppression can find hope in the Church of the East's later flourishing.
That hope is a measure of the same hope Simeon himself refused to surrender on the day of his death.
